title: Shatter
theme: She loses her baby, her name and her home — then signs a marriage contract that ends the day he is sentenced.
start_state: Port Merrow, the Glass House on the bluff that Grant Whitlock built for her. Nora Quinn is thirty-one, five months pregnant and high-risk; Dr. Brandt has prescribed prenatal medication. At nineteen she learned to blow glass from Walter Pell at Pell Glassworks on Kiln Row; in six years of marriage she hasn't touched a furnace. The Forever vase she blew at twenty-five as a wedding gift to her husband has become Whitlock Home's best seller, and her name isn't on the label. Her mother-in-law, Peg Whitlock, comes once a week to complain the soup is bland and the nursery window is too big. In episode 1 she dreams the Glass House shatters from the roof down, pane by pane, without a sound; a crooked glass bird falls and a hand catches it. She wakes, takes her pill, and says: “My pill tastes sweet today.”
end_state: The sweet pill is explained (m01: not the medication Dr. Brandt prescribed but a lookalike sugar tablet; the hospital pharmacy pickup log shows the real pills were collected every month, signed for by Grant Whitlock). The signature on the property agreement is explained (m02: traced from the signature on her pre-marriage design sketches — every stroke hesitates and the flick at the end is missing; it is dated the night she was under anesthesia at Merrow General, and the transfer of the Forever design rights was traced by the same hand; the court-appointed examiner confirms the forgery, the court freezes the transfers of the Glass House and the accounts, and the forgery charge is filed). Why Peg left with her is explained (m03: the day Nora came home from the hospital, Peg found a confectionery receipt in her son's car — “Prop tablets, qty 100” — and overheard him on the phone, “That's taken care of”; thirty-four years ago she sat alone all night in the same hospital's hallway). Nora lost the baby in the seventh-floor hallway at Merrow General (only the hallway, a half-knitted baby hat and the flickering light at the end). The day she came home the locks were changed; attorney Leonard Fisk handed her the property agreement she had “signed,” giving Grant the house, the accounts and the Forever design rights, while Sienna Vale had workers hanging curtains in the Glass House. She took only her mother's glass block, the Keepsake, and Peg packed a suitcase and left with her. Deputy Prosecutor Marcus Reyes declined to file on her first report (“Half a pill isn't enough”). Elias Ashford handed her the three clauses outside the Harborview Motor Inn; she signed them and filed for divorce. Ninety days later, at Merrow County Superior Court, the judge entered the divorce decree — “I'll sign the divorce. The house — I'll see you in court.” — and across the hall at the County Clerk she and Elias took out a marriage licence, Peg and Bev from the motel as witnesses. Grant folded Sienna's marriage application into his pocket: “Some other day.” At the launch of the new Forever collection she used the spotlight to reveal a line of bubbles in the vase's base — her initials and their wedding date; in six years he had never once turned it over. Elias leased her the abandoned Pell Glassworks on Kiln Row; she recognized the place she had apprenticed at nineteen, and he said, “Bought it at a sheriff's sale.” Furnace No. 3 was lit for the first time in twelve years and the studio was named Remelt; the blind competition for the ferry terminal chandelier brought in the first commission; a glass-tube case tracker went up on the studio wall, its bead pushed from Report to Charges, and the first two panels went up on the evidence wall. In the last episode Grant walks into Remelt Studio for the first time, glances at the evidence wall and smiles: “Two panels of glass. Drop it, Nor. You can't beat me alone.” By the furnace, Elias turns, pulls off his heat glove: an old burn scar across the back of his left hand. Grant's smile freezes: “…You.” Elias says: “Hello, Sales. Twelve years.” Nora's blowpipe stops mid-air — only people from Pell's ever called him that.

episodes.title: My Pill Tastes Sweet Today
episodes.youtube_title: Five months pregnant, she bit her pill. Why was it sweet?
episodes.logline: Five months pregnant, Nora Quinn only wants to carry her baby safely to term. But the pill her husband left out this morning tastes sweet, and by night the phone by her bed is gone.
episodes.hook: A silent dream: the Glass House on the bluff breaks apart pane by pane from the roof down, shards hanging in midair; a crooked glass bird falls, and a hand reaches into frame and catches it. She wakes to a glass of warm water and one pill. She bites down and frowns: “My pill tastes sweet today.”
episodes.mid_hook: Afternoon. The doorbell. Cole, Grant's driver, stands there in white gloves: “Mr. Whitlock sent me.” “Your phone's going in for repair.” She hands it over. The door shuts, and the whole glass house goes quiet except for the waves.
extra_hooks: Peg stands in the nursery doorway, staring at the floor-to-ceiling window: “Window that big.” “The whole street can see in.” She picks the half-knitted hat up off the couch: “Stitches are loose.” “It'll come out too big.”
episodes.conflict: She wants to do what Dr. Brandt told her: rest, take her pills, get through the days. But the pill tastes wrong. She calls Grant and he laughs it off, “They changed the coating, babe,” then says her phone keeps dropping calls and he'll send his driver to take it in for repair. Peg makes her weekly visit to find fault: the soup's bland, the nursery window's too big.
episodes.turn: After a whole day of nitpicking, Peg leaves, and there's a pot of soup in the fridge with a note on the lid: “Salt's on you.” On TV, an ad: Grant cradling the Forever vase she blew at twenty-five, bowing slightly; the label reads only “Whitlock Home.” She looks at the half pill again. One letter of the imprint is fainter than usual.

cliffhanger.text: Past midnight, a cramp jolts her awake. She reaches for the nightstand. Empty. The phone never came back. She edges along the cold glass wall, and every pane reflects only her, alone.
cliffhanger.question: No phone. Who does she call?

episodes.spectacle: In the dream the Glass House splits pane by pane from the roof down, the shards hanging in the air without falling; a crooked glass bird drops through them and a hand catches it cleanly.
episodes.glamour_shot: Morning light through the floor-to-ceiling glass: Nora in a cream knit sweater, long hair loose, holds the half pill up to the window and squints at the imprint, her profile as still as glass.
general_payoffs: She wraps the spat-out half pill in a tissue and tucks it in her coat pocket instead of throwing it away

locations: The Glass House (bedroom, dining table, nursery)

episodes.title: The Light at the End of the Hall
episodes.youtube_title: No phone, no husband. A stranger stopped and made the call
episodes.logline: She drags herself to the front door for help, and a stranger whose face she never sees calls an ambulance. In the seventh-floor hallway at Merrow General, the one who comes isn't her husband. It's a doctor saying “I'm so sorry.”
episodes.hook: She pulls on her coat, the half-knitted hat still in her fist, and inches along the glass wall to the front door. Rain hits her face. She grabs the lamppost by the door; its light flickers.
episodes.mid_hook: A car brakes hard on the drive, headlights cutting through the rain. We see only a left hand dialing 911, an old burn scar across the back: “Glass House, on the bluff.” “Pregnant woman.” “Hurry.”
extra_hooks: Merrow General, the seventh-floor hallway with no windows. At the far end a light flickers. On the bench beneath it, a soaked figure sits down, face in shadow.
episodes.conflict: She has to hold on until someone comes. But her phone is gone, she's alone in the house, and her husband can't be reached all night.
episodes.turn: The one who saves her isn't her husband. It's someone whose face she can't make out. In the ambulance a voice keeps saying in her ear, “Stay awake.” The voice is all she remembers.

cliffhanger.text: Dr. Brandt crouches by her bed and pauses a beat: “I'm so sorry.” Nora is still clutching the hat. Nurse Kim gently slips it into a paper bag. At the end of the hall, the light flickers again.
cliffhanger.question: Where was her husband?

episodes.spectacle: A rainy night on the drive: the lamppost at the Glass House door flickering, headlights breaking through the rain to stop at her feet; Merrow General's seventh floor, a long windowless hallway, the light at its end going bright, dark, bright.
episodes.glamour_shot: Rain runs down her long hair as she holds the lamppost and looks up; the headlights wash her pale profile cold blue.
general_payoffs: A stranger calls the ambulance for her
The hat stays in her hand the whole way and ends up in the hospital's paper bag
locations: The Glass House front door and lamppost

episodes.title: We're Still Young
episodes.youtube_title: She waited alone till dawn. He said: “We're still young.”
episodes.logline: Nora needs to know where her husband was that night. He arrives at dawn and says he was at his mom's and his phone died. But his phone keeps lighting up.
episodes.hook: Dawn. The elevator opens. Grant's umbrella is still dripping, his rimless glasses fogged. He takes her hand, his voice warm as a keynote: “We're still young.”
episodes.mid_hook: Nurse Kim changes the IV and says softly: “The man who called 911?” “Not your husband.” “Some man.” “He didn't leave a name.” Nora turns to Grant. He's looking down, wiping his glasses.
extra_hooks: He says: “I was at Mom's.” “My phone died.” The words are barely out when the phone in his jacket buzzes. Then again.
episodes.conflict: She needs to know where her husband was and why she couldn't reach him. All he gives her is “I was at Mom's” and “My phone died.”
episodes.turn: She thought he was just late. One line from the nurse, “Not your husband,” and a phone that's supposedly dead but won't stop buzzing: for the first time, she knows he's lying.

cliffhanger.text: He steps out to the nurses' station. On the nightstand his phone lights up: “Got the curtain measurements. —S.” She stares at that S. He comes back and, without a word, flips the phone face down.
cliffhanger.question: Who is S.? Why the curtains?

episodes.spectacle: The seventh-floor hallway at dawn, the light at the end still flickering; a dripping black umbrella propped by the door, a small puddle on the floor reflecting the flicker.
episodes.glamour_shot: Dawn light slices through the blinds onto her pale profile and the long hair spread on the pillow. She watches that phone, and for the first time her eyes go cold.
general_payoffs: She learns his dead phone was a lie
She learns the ambulance was called by a man who left no name

episodes.title: The Old One Couldn't Be Fixed
episodes.youtube_title: Her new phone had no numbers in it. Not even her doctor's
episodes.logline: Nora wants to tell Grant about the sweet pill, but he hands her a new phone first, and every line she had to the outside world is gone.
episodes.hook: He pockets the face-down phone and pulls a new box from a paper bag: “The old one couldn't be fixed.” “Got you a new one.” She turns it on. The contacts list is empty.
episodes.mid_hook: She says: “That pill.” “It was sweet.” He smiles and tucks the blanket around her: “You're exhausted.” “The doctor said you'd overthink things.”
episodes.conflict: She wants her husband to hear “The pill was sweet.” With one “You're exhausted” he takes the words away, and he swaps out her phone, her number, and every person she could call for help.
episodes.turn: She thinks the new phone is thoughtful. Then she finds her old number disconnected; Dr. Brandt, her friends, her old studio, all gone. Her only line to the world now runs through him.

cliffhanger.text: He gets up, lifts her coat off the chair, and slides a hand into the pocket: “I'll take this home and wash it.” “Bring you a clean one tomorrow.” His fingers stop on the wad of tissue.
cliffhanger.question: Will he find the half pill?

episodes.title: The Wall at the End of the Hall
episodes.youtube_title: Mother-in-law packed for a month. Then she saw the wall
episodes.logline: Nora has to keep the half pill in her pocket. Her mother-in-law arrives with a suitcase, sharp-tongued as ever, then stands a long time at the wall at the end of the hall.
episodes.hook: She clamps a hand over the coat: “I'm cold.” Grant pauses, then smiles and lets go, draping the coat back over her shoulders: “Okay.” “No washing.” Her hand slides into the pocket and closes tight around the tissue.
episodes.mid_hook: Peg steps off the elevator with a big suitcase and a thermos of soup. She walks right past the room, down to the flickering light at the end of the hall. She looks at the blank wall and touches it once.
extra_hooks: Peg comes in and plants the thermos on the table: “Drink.” “It's bland.” “You like bland, right?” The suitcase holding a month of clothes stands beside the bed.
episodes.conflict: Before discharge she has to protect the half pill in her pocket and deal with her mother-in-law. Grant books her a car home and drives off ahead with his mother and the luggage.
episodes.turn: She thought Peg came to gloat. Instead Peg packed a month of clothes to move into the Glass House and cook for her. And in her son's car, something drains the color from Peg's face.

cliffhanger.text: In Grant's car, Peg opens the glovebox for a tissue and her fingers touch a folded receipt. One glance and she freezes. Her son watches her in the rearview mirror: “Mom?” “What's wrong?” She folds it small and tucks it into her ledger: “Nothing.”
cliffhanger.question: What did Peg find in the car?

episodes.spectacle: At the end of the windowless seventh-floor hallway, an old woman in a worn cardigan stands under the flickering light, palm flat against a blank wall; each time the light blinks, her shadow breaks.
episodes.glamour_shot: Nora sits on the edge of the bed, coat pulled around her shoulders, watching Peg's back through the doorway, long hair over her cream sweater, her wariness slowly turning to confusion.
general_payoffs: The half pill is safe, still in her coat pocket

episodes.title: They Changed the Locks
episodes.youtube_title: Her key won't turn. His lawyer says she signed it all away
episodes.logline: Home from the hospital, Nora's key won't turn. Her husband's lawyer is waiting inside with a property agreement she never signed, and it carries her signature.
episodes.hook: The car stops at the top of the drive. She climbs out holding the hospital bag and puts her key in the Glass House lock. It won't turn. She tries again. The lock is new, so shiny it hurts.
episodes.mid_hook: The door opens from inside. A man with slicked-back hair and gold-rimmed glasses, fountain pen in hand: “Mrs. Whitlock.” “Leonard Fisk, Grant's attorney.” “Two documents.” “One for you to sign.” “One you already signed.”
extra_hooks: In the living room, installers are hanging heavy grey curtains over the floor-to-ceiling glass. A woman with short hair and red lipstick directs them in heels: “Left side, a little more.” “This house is too see-through.”
episodes.conflict: She wants into her own home. Leonard Fisk blocks the door: divorce papers waiting for her signature, and a separate property agreement saying she already gave Grant everything.
episodes.turn: She thought the lock was broken. The whole house is no longer hers: the house, the accounts, even the design rights to the Forever vase she blew, all on a page with her signature. And the woman hanging curtains is the S. from the text: Sienna Vale, brand director at Whitlock Home.

cliffhanger.text: The last page of the property agreement: her name on the signature line, in her handwriting. Fisk adjusts his glasses: “The house, the accounts.” “The Forever design rights.” “You gave Grant all of it.” She stares at the signature: “I never signed that.”
cliffhanger.question: Then who signed it?

episodes.title: Ten Minutes
episodes.youtube_title: Ten minutes to pack. No jewelry. Just her mother's glass
episodes.logline: Nora has ten minutes to take what's hers. No jewelry, no money. Only her sketches from before the marriage and her mother's glass piece, the Keepsake block.
episodes.hook: Fisk taps the signature line: “It's in writing.” She says: “I want to see him.” Sienna signs the curtain delivery slip left-handed, without looking up: “Grant's busy.”
episodes.mid_hook: At the nursery door, an installer lifts a curtain rod: “This one too?” Sienna: “That one too.” Nora stops in the doorway and doesn't go in. The big window disappears inch by inch behind grey fabric.
extra_hooks: A suitcase stands by the front door, zipper half open, her clothes folded by someone else's hands. Fisk checks his watch: “Ten minutes.” “Personal items only.”
episodes.conflict: Fisk gives her ten minutes for personal items. Everything in the house has been listed as community property; in ten minutes she has to decide what truly belongs to her.
episodes.turn: Fisk says everything is community property, but the block on the shelf isn't anywhere on his list. Grant never thought it was worth anything. She picks up the Keepsake block, then pulls a thin folder from the bottom shelf in the study: “Sketches from before the wedding.” “Mine.”

episodes.title: I'm Going with Her
episodes.youtube_title: She walked down the hill. Her mother-in-law followed
episodes.logline: Nora won't sign and rolls her suitcase down the drive. Grant waits in his car for her to give in, and the first one out of that car is his mother.
episodes.hook: She pulls her hand back: “I never signed that one.” “I don't accept it.” “And this one?” “I won't sign.” She takes her suitcase, holds the glass block, and walks past Fisk.
episodes.mid_hook: Grant's car waits at the bottom of the drive, engine running. The window slides halfway down, phone still in his hand: “Nor, stop this.” “Sign it.” “I'll write you a check.” She doesn't break stride.
extra_hooks: In the passenger seat, Peg holds her ledger and looks through the windshield at the Glass House up the hill as its curtains close one by one.
episodes.conflict: Grant waits in the car for her signature and offers money. All she has is a suitcase and a block of glass: no money, no phone numbers, nowhere to go.
episodes.turn: We expect her to be pushed back up the hill to sign. She doesn't even look at the car. And no one expects the mother-in-law in the passenger seat to open her door, haul her own month's suitcase out of the trunk, and go after her down the hill.

episodes.hook: Rosa plants herself, ladle up, grey crop, old silver bangle. "Get my sign in the shot. Free advertising!" One by one the cameras drop and back off.
episodes.mid_hook: She pulls Nora into the shack and sets down a bowl with a thunk. "Eat." At the stove she looks at Nora a beat too long. Says nothing.
extra_hooks: Sparks slurps chowder in the doorway. "Extra crackers?" Rosa doesn't turn around. "Get 'em yourself."
episodes.conflict: Nora wants to thank this stranger and find out why she helped. Rosa will give her chowder and not one answer.
episodes.turn: Nora thinks Rosa just hates reporters. But that look isn't for a stranger. It's someone checking a face she saw a long time ago.

cliffhanger.text: Nora finishes and stands to thank her. Rosa, back turned, stirs the pot. "You've gotten thin." Nora stops at the door. "Have we met?" Rosa doesn't turn. "Finish your bowl first."

episodes.title: I Was One Day Late
episodes.youtube_title: Peg finally hands over a receipt, and what her son said
episodes.logline: At the evidence wall, Peg tells what she has hidden for two months: the receipt in her son's car, the phone call that night, and her own night in the same hallway thirty-four years ago.
episodes.hook: Peg flattens the slip on the light box. A receipt from a confectionery that makes prop candy. Item: “Replica tablets.” Qty: “100.” In the corner, a number: 0417-100. “The day you left the hospital.” “It was in his car.”
episodes.mid_hook: “That night,” “he slept at my place.” “Out on the porch, on the phone.” “I heard him say,” “That thing's taken care of.”
extra_hooks: She takes off her reading glasses. “Thirty-four years ago,” “I sat in that same hallway.” “All night.” “His father never came.”
episodes.conflict: Hand this over and she is a mother testifying against her own son. She has kept it two months, watching her daughter-in-law dig and hold on alone.
episodes.turn: You think Peg kept quiet to protect her son. She kept quiet because she already knew, and couldn't admit the boy she raised could do it. She left with Nora because thirty-four years ago, nobody left with her.

cliffhanger.text: Peg pushes the receipt across the table. “I'm not helping you.” “I'm helping that baby.” A long pause. “I was one day late.” Nora stands and hugs her, for the first time. Peg goes stiff, then lifts a hand and pats her back once.
cliffhanger.question: Can this receipt sink him?

episodes.spectacle: The light box shines up through a crumpled receipt; “Replica tablets”, “100” and the number in the corner glow as if they were etched in glass.
episodes.glamour_shot: The moment she hugs Peg, her shoulder-length hair against Peg's worn cardigan, the furnace lights them from behind and their two shadows merge into one.
general_payoffs: Why Peg left with her is revealed: the day Nora left the hospital, Peg found a receipt in Grant's car from a confectionery that makes prop candy, “Replica tablets, 100 count”, and that night heard him on the phone: “That thing's taken care of.” Thirty-four years ago she sat alone all night in the same Merrow General hallway

episodes.title: Number Three Can't Go Cold
episodes.youtube_title: The ferry night moves up, and the old furnace man goes down
episodes.logline: The ferry terminal moves its maiden voyage up a week with twelve blue panels still unblown; that same night Gus throws out his back hauling cullet alone, and Number Three can't be allowed to go cold.
episodes.hook: Fiona stands in Remelt's doorway with the spec binder. “The maiden voyage” “moved up to next Friday.” Sparks looks at the half-built chandelier on the rack. “We've still got twelve…”
episodes.mid_hook: Midnight. Gus hauls a sack of cullet alone, locks up halfway bent, and eases himself down to the floor against the furnace. “My back.”
extra_hooks: She calls a car to take him to a doctor; Gus grabs her sleeve and won't go. “The furnace.” “Can't go cold.” “It goes cold,” “the brick cracks.”
episodes.conflict: Twelve panels in eight days. If Number Three goes cold, its twelve-year-old brick could crack through. Only Gus knows how to tend it, and she still can't go near a hot furnace.
episodes.turn: She thought the deadline was the hard part. It's people: the only blower is a twenty-year-old apprentice, the man who keeps the fire is down, and she can't touch the furnace.

cliffhanger.text: Gus on the floor, gripping her sleeve. “If I go,” “who watches the fire” “tonight?” Number Three roars on. The clock on the wall hits ten.
cliffhanger.question: Who keeps Number Three lit?

episodes.spectacle: In Number Three's firelight a sack of cullet spills across the floor, blue and clear shards everywhere, reflecting an old man sitting on the ground.
episodes.glamour_shot: She crouches beside Gus with a hand on his back, her apron dusted white, and looks back at the roaring furnace; for the first time her eyes show a flicker of panic.

episodes.title: The Man in the Heat Gloves
episodes.youtube_title: Who watches the furnace? Her contract husband walks in
episodes.logline: With no one to tend Number Three, Elias shows up at night in heat gloves; he tends the fire and never touches her chandelier while Nora calls the moves and Sparks blows panel after panel, seven nights straight.
episodes.hook: Ten p.m. The steel door swings open: Elias in work clothes, thick heat gloves on both hands. “Gus called me.” Gus lifts a hand from the cot. “Mr. Ashford.” “The fire's yours.”

cliffhanger.text: Dawn on the seventh day, twenty-three blue panels on the rack. She hands Sparks the blowpipe. “Last one.” “All yours.” “I won't call it.” Sparks's grip on the pipe shakes.

episodes.title: The Court Will Give It Back
episodes.youtube_title: Her chandelier lights the terminal. Then her ex calls
episodes.logline: Maiden voyage night: twenty-four blue panels light up the terminal and the blind-review envelope says “Remelt”; onstage Grant can only say congratulations, and afterward he calls with an offer.
episodes.hook: The terminal hall goes dark, and twenty-four blue panels light up at once, hanging like dawn waves rolling in over the harbor. The whole room looks up. Nobody says a word.
episodes.mid_hook: Fiona takes the stage. “It was a blind review.” “We only learned who” “when we opened the envelope.” “Remelt.” Every head turns to find the designer; she's at the very back in her work jacket.
extra_hooks: Sponsor's remarks. Grant has just said “supporting local design” when a reporter calls out: “The designer's your ex-wife.” “Any thoughts?” His smile stalls a beat. “…Congratulations to her.”
Before the crowd leaves, she presses a wedding ring into Peg's palm. “The first ferry check.” “I got it back.” Peg grumbles, “Who asked you to?” and puts it on right there.
episodes.conflict: It's her first work hung in a public space, and Grant is the sponsor: he means to stand under her light and talk up his brand.
episodes.turn: Grant thinks the sponsor's podium lets him make the chandelier his. Once the blind-review envelope is opened, the whole room knows who made it, and all he can say on camera is “Congratulations.”

cliffhanger.text: In the car home, her phone rings. Grant. “Drop the case” “and you get the house back.” “I don't need you to give it back.” “The court will.” She hangs up. The screen lights again, a text: “Then I'll come to you.” “Face to face.”

episodes.title: He Walks In
episodes.youtube_title: Her ex's car turns onto Kiln Row. She leaves the door open
episodes.logline: Grant's car turns onto Kiln Row; Nora teaches Sparks the wrist turn with an empty blowpipe while Elias keeps the furnace with his back to the door. She doesn't shut the steel door.
episodes.hook: 7:58 p.m. Her phone lights up. Theo: “His car” “just turned onto Kiln Row.”
episodes.mid_hook: The engine dies outside. Dress shoes on gravel, step by step. Sparks, low: “Should I” “shut the door?” “Let him in.” “Let him look.”
extra_hooks: Dr. Brandt's ban still holds, so her blowpipe is empty; she's only teaching Sparks the wrist turn. “Wrist.” “Don't stop.” At the furnace mouth, Elias, gloved, back to the door, shovels in cullet.
episodes.conflict: She'll face him on her own ground: no shouting, no begging, no one speaking for her. All she has is a wall with two panels and an empty blowpipe.
episodes.turn: You expect her to shut the door and hide behind someone. She leaves it open and keeps teaching Sparks the wrist turn. What she wants him to see first isn't the evidence. It's her, back at the furnace.

cliffhanger.text: The footsteps stop outside. The steel door creaks open a crack, and a hand with a glass cufflink rests on it: streetlight on one side, furnace glow on the other.
cliffhanger.question: What does he want inside?

episodes.spectacle: Remelt's steel door swings slowly open; the Kiln Row streetlight outside and Number Three's fire inside meet at the threshold, where a man in a pale suit stands on the line.
episodes.glamour_shot: She holds a cold blowpipe between the furnace and the door, shoulder-length hair, work apron, goggles pushed up; when the door creaks she doesn't turn around, and her wrist keeps turning.
general_payoffs: She doesn't shut the door; she waits for him on her own ground
Grant comes in person; his car stops outside Remelt

episodes.title: Hello, Sales. Twelve Years.
episodes.youtube_title: Her ex mocks two panels. Then the man at the furnace turns
episodes.logline: Grant looks at two panels of glass, tells Nora to drop the case and says she can't beat him alone; he never sees it coming when the figure at the furnace turns around and brings back his name from twelve years ago.
episodes.hook: Grant's first time inside Remelt. He takes in the brick, the bead stopped at Charges, stops at the evidence wall, taps the first panel with his glass cufflink and smiles. “Two panels of glass.” “Drop it, Nor.” “You can't beat me alone.”
episodes.mid_hook: He steps closer, voice soft. “You think Elias” “is helping you” “out of kindness?” Her blowpipe keeps turning. “I know.” “I'm using him too.”
extra_hooks: She looks at the twelve slots. “Twelve.” “The day they're full,” “you get sentenced.” He laughs. “Twelve?” “You don't even have a third.”
episodes.conflict: Grant wants the case dropped tonight. He has lawyers, money and the press; she has two panels of glass. She has to show him she won't drop it and isn't afraid, without knowing what lies between him and the man at the furnace.
episodes.turn: Grant thinks he came to tidy up an ex-wife. He needles her, laughs at her two panels, and never once notices the figure at the furnace until that man turns around.

cliffhanger.text: At the furnace, Elias turns and pulls off his heat glove: an old burn scar across the back of his left hand. Grant's smile freezes. “…You.” Elias: “Hello, Sales.” “Twelve years.” Nora's blowpipe stops mid-air. Only people from Pell's ever called him that.
cliffhanger.question: Who was Elias at Pell's?

episodes.spectacle: Number Three's fire pours out of the furnace mouth onto a left hand just stripped of its heat glove, an old burn scar across the back; behind it, on the red brick, the two engraved panels catch the same fire.
episodes.glamour_shot: Elias turns at the fire and pulls off the heat glove finger by finger; under the rolled cuff the old scar on the back of his left hand shows, and his eyes behind the lenses are locked on Grant.
general_payoffs: Grant sets foot in Remelt for the first time and sees the two panels
